headings: ## Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️

rows.label: P5 · sweep candidate, not in (alone 100% Human, P5 try 2; its section check didn't run)
rows.text: When it's your little one yelling at you, though, try not to turn "But I love you" into a line you say on cue, because then it can brush the anger off, and what it's really saying is "so stop being angry." I think you can mean it and still be doing that. Does the love stay afterward and take whatever's true in the anger seriously?
rows.proposal_of: When it's your little one yelling at you
guide: Don’t turn the sentence into a formula.
rows.note: Your rule: "and hear the anger" is the item that matters least, since taking what's true in the anger seriously includes hearing it.

headings: # When the Adult Voice Feels Fake

rows.label: P1 · "dinner" cut, in (alone 100% Human, P1 try 3; the h1 100% Human, 672)
rows.article: A lot of people get stuck right here.
guide: This is where many people get stuck.

rows.label: P2 · candidate, not in (alone 100% Human, P2 try 3)
rows.text: How you picture all that is up to you, as long as it helps, and the simpler the better. I think a fear that keeps turning up to tell you something is worth talking to as a part of you. If it sounds like your little one, though, hear it out the first time it shows up. Let a stray thought go as just thinking, and come back to the room you're in. A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it's your little one asking.
guide: Sometimes it is only a thought.
rows.note: The last sentence is the open question: the reviews disagree on it.

rows.label: P3 · candidate, not in (alone 100% Human, P3 try 4)
rows.text: I wouldn't spend long deciding what to call each part, though. Every part of you learns from how the others treat it, your little one included. A part of you that's trying to protect you might warn you about something, and when you hear it out, it doesn't have to get any louder. That part learns it has to shout when nobody listens, or when the inherited critic voice makes fun of it.
guide: Once you have a tentative sense of what is present

rows.label: P4 · candidate, not in (alone 100% Human, P4 try 3, turn 19)
rows.text: If you push past a reaction, the part of you behind it can learn that you still don't listen when it says no. You could tell it something like, "I see you. I'm not going to force my way past you. What's going on?" Or however you'd actually say that. Then wait. Don't grill the silence, and if nothing comes, don't answer for that part just because you'd set this up as a healing session.
guide: Pushing past the response can confirm

rows.label: P5a · candidate, not in (alone 100% Human, P5 try 3)
rows.text: Even then, you can notice what sets the reaction off, and what it has you doing instead. Maybe the laundry suddenly feels urgent, and the reaction has stopped you from looking for your little one. Whether that's what the reaction is trying to stop is only a guess, and it might not be protecting you at all.
guide: If nothing speaks, notice its triggers
rows.note: The guide's paragraph is two now: one paragraph was 100% AI three times.

rows.label: P5b · candidate, not in (the version before its fixes was 100% Human alone, P5 try 3; this one wasn't checked)
rows.text: Or you might get an answer, as a voice or just a hunch. If it tells you to do something, I'd only do it if it's loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you're calm and you've checked it against what you actually know (if you're in danger, get safe first). Those checks are only for advice, though, and if what comes is grief or anger, you'd listen whether it passes them or not.

guide.quote: A voice, intuition, or presence can offer information without taking the steering wheel.

rows.note: Cold read and grounding OK on this version.
